mcqs.question: Why does cache design focus so heavily on reducing misses rather than further speeding up hits?
options: Because hits are already free and cost nothing to serve
Because hardware can't make hits any faster than they already are
Because hits don't use any power, so there's nothing to optimize there
Because a miss is typically 10-100x slower than a hit, so misses dominate total access time even when rare
mcqs.explanation: Hits are fast but not free, and hardware absolutely can and does optimize hit latency. The real reason misses dominate is the sheer size of the penalty gap — a small fraction of misses can outweigh a large majority of cheap hits in total time.

mcqs.question: A cache has a hit time of 2 cycles, a miss rate of 5%, and a miss penalty of 100 cycles. What is its AMAT?
options: 7 cycles
2 cycles
100 cycles
102 cycles
mcqs.explanation: AMAT = hit time + miss rate x miss penalty = 2 + (0.05 x 100) = 2 + 5 = 7 cycles. Confusing this with the raw miss penalty (100) or ignoring the hit-time term are the common errors.

mcqs.question: In an address trace against an initially empty cache, why is the very first access to any given address always a miss?
options: Because empty caches are disabled until warmed up by the OS
Because there's nothing yet in the cache for that address to match — a miss is unavoidable on first touch, regardless of locality
Because the first access always targets the wrong cache set
Because cold caches use a different, slower placement policy
mcqs.explanation: This is the compulsory/cold miss: no amount of locality helps the very first reference to an address, since it was never fetched before. It has nothing to do with set placement or a special "cold mode" — those aren't real mechanisms.

mcqs.question: Design A has a 99% hit rate with a 400-cycle miss penalty. Design B has a 90% hit rate with a 50-cycle miss penalty. Both have equal hit time. Which has the lower miss-driven AMAT contribution (miss rate x miss penalty)?
options: They are always identical regardless of the numbers involved
Design B, since a 90% hit rate needs less hardware and is always cheaper
Design A, since its miss contribution is 0.01 x 400 = 4 cycles versus Design B's 0.10 x 50 = 5 cycles
Hit rate alone determines the winner; the miss penalty is irrelevant
mcqs.explanation: Design A's miss contribution (0.01 x 400 = 4 cycles) edges out Design B's (0.10 x 50 = 5 cycles) here, but the margin is close — a modest change to either penalty flips the winner. The lesson: the higher hit-rate design isn't automatically better, and "cheaper hardware" isn't a performance argument. You must compute both terms, never read hit rate alone as the verdict.

mcqs.question: Why do careful benchmarks typically discard the first iteration of a loop before measuring timing?
options: The CPU clock hasn't stabilized yet during the first iteration
The first iteration runs against a cold cache, so its misses reflect one-time cache-fill cost rather than the algorithm's steady-state behavior
The compiler hasn't finished compiling the loop by the first iteration
The first iteration always executes on a different CPU core than later ones
mcqs.explanation: A cold cache guarantees misses on first touch regardless of the algorithm's real locality, so timing that pass measures cache-fill cost rather than the routine's steady-state speed. Clock stabilization, compilation, and core migration aren't the mechanism here — cache warmth is.
